modules.name: Clock
modules.header:
Reading a clock, and waiting on one.
`clock_gettime` arrived on Darwin in macOS 10.12, later than everywhere else, which is why `GetTimeOfDay` is still
here: it is the call that works on every release this package could run on. Its microsecond resolution is the
price.

modules.name: Dynamic
modules.header:
Loading a shared object at run time, and finding a symbol inside it.
The entry points are libSystem's, like everything else on this system; there is no separate loader library to
link.

modules.name: Entropy
modules.header:
Unpredictable bytes, from the system's own generator.
Darwin's generator is always seeded, never blocks, and cannot fail, which is why the call it is reached through
returns nothing at all. There is no short count to loop over and no error to check — the only such source among
the four supported systems.

modules.name: Errors
modules.header:
How a libSystem call reports failure, and the numbers it reports.
Darwin reports the way C does: the call returns `-1` and leaves a positive number in the thread's `errno`, which
is reached through the `__error` accessor rather than as a variable. That is two different things for a caller to
look at, so `Normalize` folds them into the one convention the Linux and FreeBSD packages already use — a value,
or a small negative error number — and `IsError` and `Errno` then read the result the same way on all three.
The names keep the system's own spelling. The values are Darwin's, which agree with FreeBSD's more often than with
Linux's but match neither completely.

modules.name: File
modules.header:
Reading and writing through a file descriptor, and the three descriptors a process starts with.
Each wrapper folds libSystem's `-1`-and-`errno` reporting into the one normalized value the Linux and FreeBSD
packages already use, so a caller reads all three the same way. A short count is not an error and not an end of
file — only a zero-length read means the source has ended.
The descriptor constants are annotated `int32` rather than `FileDescriptor`, because a `const` cannot name a type
alias declared in another file of the package.

modules.name: LibSystem
modules.header:
The Darwin ABI: libSystem's own entry points, under the symbols it exports.
**Apple does not support calling the kernel directly.** The trap numbers are private, they have changed between
releases, and a binary that issues its own `syscall` or `svc` is not a binary Apple undertakes to keep running --
on Apple Silicon the trap interface is not reachable from ordinary code at all. libSystem is the ABI, and this
package binds it. That is the difference between this package and the Linux and FreeBSD ones, which do call the
kernel directly because those kernels publish a stable numbering.
Every declaration here reports failure the way C does: `-1` and a positive `errno`. The wrappers elsewhere in this
package fold that into one value with `Errors::Normalize`, so nothing above them has to look in two places.

modules.name: Memory
modules.header:
Mapping and unmapping address space.
There is no `Brk` here. Darwin's `brk` and `sbrk` have been unavailable to 64-bit code since the beginning, and
the previous version of this package declared one anyway, through a trap number that was never valid on Apple
Silicon. Mapping is the only way to get address space on this system.

modules.name: Process
modules.header: What a process can ask or say about itself.

modules.name: Types
modules.header:
The Darwin ABI's own types: what a libSystem call takes and gives back.
These follow the LP64 data model every supported Apple target uses, so a `long` is 64 bits and the widths below do
not vary by architecture.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_REALTIME`: wall-clock time, which can jump when the system clock is set.
doc.markdown: `CLOCK_REALTIME`: wall-clock time, which can jump when the system clock is set.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`: time since boot, which never goes backwards.
doc.markdown:
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC`: time since boot, which never goes backwards.
Darwin numbers this 6, where Linux uses 1 and FreeBSD uses 4. No clock identifier means the same thing on any two
of the three systems.

doc.summary: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`: like `ClockMonotonic`, but not adjusted by time synchronization.
doc.markdown: `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`: like `ClockMonotonic`, but not adjusted by time synchronization.

items.name: ClockGetTime
items.signature: pub func ClockGetTime(clockId: int32, time: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads `clockId` into `time`.
doc.markdown:
Reads `clockId` into `time`.
Callers pass an explicit address, as they do on Linux and FreeBSD: `ClockGetTime(ClockMonotonic, @time)`.
The call itself needs macOS 10.12 or later; an older release has no such symbol and the program will not launch.
`time` must be non-null and writable for a whole `Timespec`.

params.name: clockId
params.markdown: which clock to read, one of the identifiers above

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: ClockGetResolution
items.signature: pub func ClockGetResolution(clockId: int32, resolution: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads the resolution of `clockId` into `resolution`.
doc.markdown:
Reads the resolution of `clockId` into `resolution`.
The resolution is the granularity the clock advances by, not the cost of reading it and not a promise about
accuracy. Like `ClockGetTime`, it needs macOS 10.12 or later.
`resolution` must be non-null and writable for a whole `Timespec`.

params.name: clockId
params.markdown: which clock to describe, one of the identifiers above

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Reads the wall clock into `time`, to microsecond resolution.
doc.markdown:
Reads the wall clock into `time`, to microsecond resolution.
The second argument of the underlying call is an obsolete time-zone output that this passes as null.
`Timeval` has Darwin's layout: an eight-byte second count and a four-byte microsecond count, not two 64-bit
fields.
`time` must be non-null and writable for a whole `Timeval`.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Nanosleep
items.signature: pub func Nanosleep(request: *Timespec, remaining: *var Timespec) -> int64

doc.summary: Suspends the caller for the requested duration.
doc.markdown:
Suspends the caller for the requested duration.
`EINTR` with the unslept time left in `remaining` is how a signal cutting the wait short is reported.
`request` must be non-null, and its nanoseconds must be under one second.

params.name: remaining
params.markdown: receives the unslept time when a signal cut the wait short, and may be null

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: `RTLD_LAZY`: resolve a function symbol the first time it is called rather than at load.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_LAZY`: resolve a function symbol the first time it is called rather than at load.

doc.summary: `RTLD_NOW`: resolve every symbol before `dlopen` returns.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_NOW`: resolve every symbol before `dlopen` returns.

doc.summary: `RTLD_LOCAL`: keep this object's symbols to itself, which is Darwin's default.
doc.markdown:
`RTLD_LOCAL`: keep this object's symbols to itself, which is Darwin's default.
Darwin numbers this 4 and `RTLD_GLOBAL` 8, where both Linux and FreeBSD use 0 and 256. Carrying either value
between packages selects the opposite of what was meant.

doc.summary: `RTLD_GLOBAL`: make this object's symbols available to objects loaded afterwards.
doc.markdown: `RTLD_GLOBAL`: make this object's symbols available to objects loaded afterwards.

items.name: GetRandom
items.signature: pub func GetRandom(buffer: *var opaque, length: uint)

doc.summary: Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
doc.markdown:
Fills `length` bytes of `buffer` with unpredictable bytes.
`buffer` is borrowed and written; `length` is read by value. Returns nothing, because this cannot fail: the
generator is seeded before any user code runs and never blocks.
Suitable for a key, a token, or anything an adversary would like to guess.
Runs in time proportional to `length` and allocates nothing.
`buffer` must be writable for `length` bytes.

doc.summary: Folds a libSystem result and the thread's `errno` into one value.
doc.markdown:
Folds a libSystem result and the thread's `errno` into one value.
`result` is read by value. A result of `-1` becomes the negative of whatever `errno` holds; anything else is
returned unchanged. That is what makes every wrapper in this package report the way the Linux and FreeBSD ones
do, so a caller reads all three with `IsError` and `Errno`.
A call that legitimately returns `-1` would be misread, which is why nothing here wraps one.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

items.name: Read
items.signature: pub func Read(fd: FileDescriptor, buffer: *var opaque, count: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Reads up to `count` bytes from `fd` into `buffer`.
doc.markdown:
Reads up to `count` bytes from `fd` into `buffer`.
`buffer` is borrowed and written. Returns the number of bytes read, zero at end of file, or a negative error
number. A short count is ordinary.
`buffer` must be writable for `count` bytes.

params.name: count
params.markdown: how many bytes to ask for

doc.returns: the bytes read, zero at end of file, or a negative error number

items.name: Write
items.signature: pub func Write(fd: FileDescriptor, buffer: *opaque, count: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Writes up to `count` bytes from `buffer` to `fd`.
doc.markdown:
Writes up to `count` bytes from `buffer` to `fd`.
`buffer` is borrowed and read. Returns the number of bytes written, or a negative error number. A short count is
ordinary and the rest has to be written by calling again.
`buffer` must be readable for `count` bytes.
doc.returns: the bytes written, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Closes `fd` and releases what the kernel held for it.
doc.markdown:
Closes `fd` and releases what the kernel held for it.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. A failure does not mean the descriptor is still open.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: OpenAt
items.signature: pub func OpenAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, flags: int32, mode: FileMode) -> int64

doc.summary: Opens `path` relative to `directoryFd` and returns a descriptor, or a negative error number.
doc.markdown:
Opens `path` relative to `directoryFd` and returns a descriptor, or a negative error number.
`directoryFd` is `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path. `mode` is read only when `OpenCreate` is set.
`path` must be non-null and terminated. The mode is masked by the process umask.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

params.name: path
params.markdown: the path to open, as a null-terminated byte string

params.name: flags
params.markdown: the access mode and the open flags, combined with `|`

params.name: mode
params.markdown: the permission bits for a file this creates, ignored otherwise

doc.returns: the new descriptor, or a negative error number

Makes `path` the process's working directory.

Reads the text a symbolic link holds into `buffer`.

items.signature: pub func SymlinkAt(target: *char8, newDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, linkPath: *char8) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a symbolic link at `linkPath` holding `target` as its text.
doc.markdown:
Creates a symbolic link at `linkPath` holding `target` as its text.
Returns zero, or a negative error number. The target is stored, not checked: a dangling link is created as
readily as a good one, which is a property callers rely on.

params.name: target
params.markdown: the text the link will hold, which need not exist

items.name: Getdirentries64
items.signature: pub func Getdirentries64(fd: FileDescriptor, buffer: *var opaque, count: uint, position: *var int64) -> int64

doc.summary:
Reads directory entries from `fd` into `buffer`, and returns the bytes filled, zero at the end, or a negative
error number.
doc.markdown:
Reads directory entries from `fd` into `buffer`, and returns the bytes filled, zero at the end, or a negative
error number.
The buffer holds packed 64-bit-inode `dirent` records: the inode at offset 0 (8 bytes), a seek cookie at 8
(8 bytes), the record's length at 16 (2 bytes), the name's length at 18 (2 bytes), the entry type at 20
(1 byte), and the name from 21. The kernel writes as many whole records as fit.

params.name: position
params.markdown: receives the position of the block read

doc.returns: the bytes filled, zero at the end of the directory, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Flushes everything written to `fd` toward the storage device.
doc.markdown:
Flushes everything written to `fd` toward the storage device.
Returns zero, or a negative error number.
This is weaker on Darwin than everywhere else: it hands the data to the device without waiting for the device to
commit it, so a power failure can still lose a write this reported as flushed. `F_FULLFSYNC` through `fcntl` is
what actually waits, and this package does not wrap it.
doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Sets the length of the file behind `fd` to `length`.
doc.markdown:
Sets the length of the file behind `fd` to `length`.
Growing creates a hole rather than allocating, so a later write into it can still fail with `ENOSPC`.

params.name: length
params.markdown: the size the file should have afterwards

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

Removes the name `path` from its directory.
`flags` is zero for a file or `RemoveDirectory` for an empty directory. Removing a name does not free the file.
`path` must be non-null and terminated.

params.name: directoryFd

items.signature: pub func MkdirAt(directoryFd: FileDescriptor, path: *char8, mode: FileMode) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a directory named `path` with permission bits `mode`.
doc.markdown:
Creates a directory named `path` with permission bits `mode`.
Reports `EEXIST` when the name is taken.
`path` must be non-null and terminated.

params.name: directoryFd
params.markdown: the directory `path` is relative to, or `AtFdCwd` for an ordinary path

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: RenameAt
items.signature: pub func RenameAt(oldDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, oldPath: *char8, newDirectoryFd: FileDescriptor, newPath: *char8) -> int64

doc.summary: Renames `oldPath` to `newPath`, each resolved against its own directory descriptor.
doc.markdown:
Renames `oldPath` to `newPath`, each resolved against its own directory descriptor.
Within one file system this replaces any existing `newPath` atomically. Across file systems it reports `EXDEV`.
Both paths must be non-null and terminated.

params.name: newPath
params.markdown: the name to move it to

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Dup2
items.signature: pub func Dup2(oldFd: FileDescriptor, newFd: FileDescriptor) -> int64

doc.summary: Makes `newFd` a copy of `oldFd`, closing whatever `newFd` was.
doc.markdown:
Makes `newFd` a copy of `oldFd`, closing whatever `newFd` was.
Returns `newFd`, or a negative error number.

params.name: newFd
params.markdown: the number the duplicate should have

doc.returns: `newFd`, or a negative error number

doc.summary: Creates a pipe and writes its two descriptors into `descriptors`.
doc.markdown:
Creates a pipe and writes its two descriptors into `descriptors`.
The reading end lands at index zero and the writing end at index one. Darwin has no `pipe2`, so close-on-exec has
to be set afterwards through `fcntl` — which leaves a window another thread can execute through.
`descriptors` must be writable for two `int32` values.

params.name: descriptors
params.markdown: receives the read end at index zero and the write end at index one

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: The library every Darwin interface is reached through.
doc.markdown:
The library every Darwin interface is reached through.
A single dynamic library re-exporting libc, libm, libpthread and the rest; there is no separate `libc.dylib` to
link on Apple platforms.

doc.summary: Reports the system page size, in bytes.
doc.markdown:
Reports the system page size, in bytes.
Darwin's page size is not the same on every machine: Apple Silicon uses 16 KiB where x86-64 uses 4 KiB, which
is why this is asked rather than assumed. Cannot fail — a process that could not be told its own page size
could not have been started.
`Memory::QueryPageSize` is the wrapper to call; this is the raw entry point it binds, and is the only
declaration in this block that is reachable from outside the package.
doc.returns: the page size in bytes

doc.summary: `PROT_NONE`: the pages may not be touched at all.
doc.markdown: `PROT_NONE`: the pages may not be touched at all.

doc.summary: `PROT_READ`: the pages may be read.
doc.markdown: `PROT_READ`: the pages may be read.

doc.summary: `PROT_WRITE`: the pages may be written.
doc.markdown: `PROT_WRITE`: the pages may be written.

doc.summary: `PROT_EXEC`: the pages may be executed.
doc.markdown:
`PROT_EXEC`: the pages may be executed.
Apple Silicon refuses a mapping that is writable and executable at once unless the process carries the
`com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` entitlement and uses `MAP_JIT`, which this package does not wrap.

doc.summary: `MAP_SHARED`: writes are visible to other mappings of the same object and reach it.
doc.markdown: `MAP_SHARED`: writes are visible to other mappings of the same object and reach it.

doc.summary: `MAP_PRIVATE`: writes are private to this mapping and never reach the object.
doc.markdown: `MAP_PRIVATE`: writes are private to this mapping and never reach the object.

doc.summary: `MAP_FIXED`: place the mapping exactly at the requested address, replacing whatever was there.
doc.markdown: `MAP_FIXED`: place the mapping exactly at the requested address, replacing whatever was there.

doc.summary: `MAP_ANON`: the mapping is backed by zeroed pages rather than by a file.
doc.markdown: `MAP_ANON`: the mapping is backed by zeroed pages rather than by a file.

doc.summary: `MADV_FREE`: the pages may be reclaimed, and read back as zero if they are.
doc.markdown: `MADV_FREE`: the pages may be reclaimed, and read back as zero if they are.

doc.summary: `MADV_DONTNEED`: the pages are not needed soon.
doc.markdown: `MADV_DONTNEED`: the pages are not needed soon. Advisory on Darwin, as on FreeBSD.

doc.summary: `MADV_WILLNEED`: the pages will be read soon.
doc.markdown: `MADV_WILLNEED`: the pages will be read soon.

items.name: Mmap
items.signature: pub func Mmap(address: *opaque, length: uint, protection: int32, flags: int32, fd: int32, offset: uint64) -> int64

doc.summary: Creates a mapping and returns its address, or a negative error number.
doc.markdown:
Creates a mapping and returns its address, or a negative error number.
`address` is a hint unless `MapFixed` is set. `fd` is the object to map, or `-1` with `MapAnonymous`.
libSystem reports failure here as `MAP_FAILED`, which is `-1` cast to a pointer rather than a small negative
number, so the failure is folded into the same normalized form every other wrapper uses. Test the result with
`IsError`, not for a sign: a valid address may have its top bit set.
`MapFixed` replaces whatever occupies the address, including a mapping this program depends on.

params.name: address
params.markdown: a hint for where to map, or null to let the kernel choose

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes, rounded up to whole pages

params.name: protection
params.markdown: what may be done with the pages, as `Protection*` flags

params.name: fd
params.markdown: the file to map, or -1 with `MapAnonymous`

params.name: offset
params.markdown: where in the file the mapping starts

doc.returns: the mapping's address, or a negative error number

items.name: Munmap
items.signature: pub func Munmap(address: *opaque, length: uint) -> int64

doc.summary: Releases the mapping that begins at `address` and spans `length` bytes.
doc.markdown:
Releases the mapping that begins at `address` and spans `length` bytes.
Returns zero, or a negative error number.
Every pointer into the range becomes invalid.

params.name: address
params.markdown: a page-aligned address to release from

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Mprotect
items.signature: pub func Mprotect(address: *opaque, length: uint, protection: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Changes what may be done with the pages covering a range.
doc.markdown:
Changes what may be done with the pages covering a range.
`address` must be page-aligned. Returns zero, or a negative error number.
Apple Silicon refuses to make a range writable and executable at once without the JIT entitlement.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes, rounded up to whole pages

params.name: protection
params.markdown: what may be done with them afterwards

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

items.name: Madvise
items.signature: pub func Madvise(address: *opaque, length: uint, advice: int32) -> int64

doc.summary: Tells the kernel how the pages covering a range are about to be used.
doc.markdown:
Tells the kernel how the pages covering a range are about to be used.
Advice is advice, with the exception of `AdviseFree`, which actually releases.
`AdviseFree` loses whatever the range held.

params.name: length
params.markdown: how many bytes the advice covers

doc.returns: zero, or a negative error number

doc.summary: The size of a page, asked of libSystem.
doc.markdown:
The size of a page, asked of libSystem.
Darwin's page size is not the same on every machine: Apple Silicon uses 16 KiB where x86-64 uses 4 KiB, so this
is asked rather than assumed. The underlying call cannot fail, which is why this one cannot either — the
negative-error return exists so that one call shape reaches all three POSIX systems, not because Darwin has a
failure to report.
doc.returns: the page size in bytes, always positive on this system

doc.summary: Ends the calling process with `code`.
doc.markdown:
Ends the calling process with `code`.
Only the low eight bits reach a waiting parent. Does not return.
This is `_exit` rather than `exit`: nothing registered with `atexit` runs and no stream is flushed, which matches
what the Linux and FreeBSD packages do and is what a raw binding should do. A program wanting the other behaviour
should call C's `exit` through `Rux/C`.

params.name: code
params.markdown: the status to report to the parent

doc.summary: The calling process's own identifier.
doc.markdown:
The calling process's own identifier.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the calling process's identifier

doc.summary: A process identifier, as `getpid` reports one.
doc.markdown: A process identifier, as `getpid` reports one.

doc.summary: A file descriptor, as the kernel numbers one.
doc.markdown: A file descriptor, as the kernel numbers one.

doc.summary: A byte offset within a file, 64 bits on every supported Apple target.
doc.markdown: A byte offset within a file, 64 bits on every supported Apple target.

doc.summary: A file's type and permission bits.
doc.markdown:
A file's type and permission bits.
Sixteen bits here, where Linux's `mode_t` is thirty-two. The bit meanings agree; the width does not.

doc.summary: A user identifier.
doc.markdown: A user identifier.

doc.summary: A group identifier.
doc.markdown: A group identifier.

doc.summary: A duration or an instant, as seconds and nanoseconds.
doc.markdown: A duration or an instant, as seconds and nanoseconds.

doc.summary: A duration or an instant, as seconds and microseconds.
doc.markdown:
A duration or an instant, as seconds and microseconds.
Darwin's x86-64 layout is an eight-byte `time_t` followed by a four-byte `suseconds_t`, and four bytes of trailing
padding. The padding is why this is not two 64-bit fields, and why writing it as though it were corrupts nothing
but reads back a microsecond count that is half stale.
